greeting: Good morning, Bay View, and happy Saturday. Friday's 67 degrees broke a 129-year-old record, and today brings one more sunny, mild day near 65 before rain and a colder Sunday. In the news: a big manufacturer is moving its headquarters to the R1VER building on Becher Street. And a heads-up for families: MPS students are off Tuesday through Friday next week.

lead_image.alt: The glassy eight-story R1VER office building with the Michels sign on top, at the edge of the Kinnickinnic River on W. Becher Street

top.title: Modexus, the former Modine, will move its headquarters to the R1VER office building on Becher Street
top.dek: The Racine-born manufacturer plans to fill two floors, about 40,000 square feet, of the eight-story tower.
top.body:
Modexus Solutions, the company known until this week as Modine Manufacturing, is moving its corporate headquarters from Racine to the R1VER office building at 210 W. Becher St., on the south bank of the Kinnickinnic River. A permit filed with the city shows plans for about $524,000 in improvements to the building's fourth and fifth floors, roughly 40,000 square feet.

Founded in Racine in 1916, the company recently sold its automotive and commercial-vehicle businesses and now concentrates on cooling and thermal-management equipment, including systems for data centers. It has not said when the move will happen or how many employees will work there.

Modexus would join Michels Corp., which developed R1VER and occupies its top floors, and the law firm Hall Render. The same complex includes the Tribute Apartments, a stretch of public riverwalk and ground-floor neighbors Ian's Pizza, The Bridgewater Modern Grill and Casera Cafe & Bakery, so a few hundred more weekday lunch customers could be on the way.

image.alt: The glassy eight-story R1VER office building with the Michels sign on top, at the edge of the Kinnickinnic River on W. Becher Street

top.title: Friday's 67 degrees broke a record from 1897; one more mild day, then rain and a colder Sunday
top.dek: Expect sun and a high near 65 today, then overnight rain as a cold front drops temperatures Sunday.
top.body:
Milwaukee hit 67 degrees at Mitchell Airport at 2:37 p.m. Friday, one degree above the Nov. 20 record of 66 set in 1897, according to the National Weather Service's daily climate report.

Saturday should be nearly as warm: the forecast for Bay View calls for sunshine, a high near 65 and a south wind of 10 to 15 mph, with a mostly clear, mild night around 51. The record for Nov. 21 is 70, according to CBS 58's forecasters.

The weather service says a cold front will bring a round of rain overnight into Sunday morning, followed by falling temperatures and gusty winds Sunday afternoon. If there's yard work, a lakefront walk or a bike ride you've been putting off, today is the day.

image.alt: Sailboats moored off South Shore Park under a clear blue sky, with the rocky shoreline and lakefront path in the foreground (stock photo)

spotlight.title: Spotlight: Heirloom MKE
spotlight.dek: The Howell Avenue restaurant grew out of a yellow food truck, survived a fire and still serves its famous burrata
spotlight.body:
Heirloom MKE is a farm-to-table restaurant and bar at 2378 S. Howell Ave., in the storefront that was home to Lazy Susan for nine years. Nearly everything is made from scratch with ingredients from local farms and purveyors, and the menu marks which items are locally sourced and which can be made vegan or gluten-free.

It's run by Pete and Jess Ignatiev, a husband-and-wife team who describe themselves as chef and gardener. Both are restaurant-industry veterans, and they were close to opening a restaurant in early 2020 when the pandemic hit. Instead they launched Heirloom that year as a food truck, and its upscale comfort food built a following at breweries and night markets around town.

The road to Howell Avenue had a scary detour. In March 2023 the couple announced they would take over the Lazy Susan space, and in July, weeks before opening, an early-morning fire destroyed the truck while it was parked in Bay View. No one was hurt. The restaurant opened anyway on Aug. 26, 2023, in a dining room with a jade-green ceiling and wallpaper that, if you look closely, shows alien abductions.

The hand-stretched burrata salad that made the truck famous is still on the menu, along with fried cheese curds, the Heirloom burger, grilled shrimp polenta and a vegan turmeric-and-ginger cauliflower steak. The list changes with the seasons and leans on Wisconsin beers, wine and a short list of creative cocktails. Friday is fish fry night: two pieces of beer-battered cod with fries, coleslaw, tartar sauce and buttered rye.

The truck story has a happy ending, too. In July 2025, almost two years after the fire, a new yellow truck the owners call Lucille 2 hit the road; their post announcing it said "our little yellow truck is BACK." Heirloom now runs both the restaurant and the truck, and its website lists where the truck will be.

Heirloom MKE, 2378 S. Howell Ave. Open Wednesday through Saturday, 4 to 9 p.m. (closed Sunday through Tuesday); reservations recommended, walk-ins welcome. heirloommke.com, Instagram @heirloom.mke.

buzz.headline: Snow-removal waitlists already? In a record-warm November
buzz.body: A neighbor two blocks north of Humboldt Park went looking for snow-removal referrals because the company they usually hire already has a waitlist this year. The job is no small one, either: a duplex on a hill with front stairs, two porches, garage paths and four garbage and recycling carts to dig out. Friday hit 67 degrees, but around here, planning ahead is the Wisconsin way.

image.alt: A snow shovel with an aluminum blade leaning against a wall (stock photo)

buzz.headline: Buy a bike at Wheel & Sprocket, take home a Christmas tree
buzz.body: Wheel & Sprocket says it's "branching out": buy any bike at its Bay View store, or its Brookfield, Fox Point, Franklin or Delafield shops, and you get a free Christmas tree. Fair warning that strapping a spruce to a new bike is not covered in the owner's manual.

image.alt: A Wheel & Sprocket staffer in a loud print shirt holds up a bike part in front of a stack of Christmas trees, with the words Buy a bike and get the tree

buzz.headline: 17th Ward's new cocktail is called Side Piece. There's duck fat in it.
buzz.body: The KK cocktail bar rolled out a five-drink "Fall Intermission" menu this week, and the headliner is Side Piece: apple brandy washed with duck fat, plus butternut squash and a brown sugar-sage syrup. Thanksgiving dinner in a glass, more or less.

image.alt: A golden cocktail in a glass punch cup garnished with a dried orange wheel, on a dark wood bar

buzz.headline: Rush Creek Reserve sighting at Outpost Bay View
buzz.body: In an r/milwaukee thread hunting for Rush Creek Reserve, the spruce-wrapped, spoonable seasonal cheese from Wisconsin's Uplands Cheese, one commenter said they'd seen it at Outpost's Bay View store about a week earlier. We couldn't confirm what's on the shelf today, so call the KK store before you make a special trip.

image.alt: A soft, spoonable spruce-bound cheese opened to show its creamy center, similar to Rush Creek Reserve (stock photo)

buzz.body: The Avalon says it's hosting a pop-up maker market with a movie night on Friday, Dec. 4, with local vendors Good Shit Video, Chippy's, Lion's Tooth and 4 of 4 Creative. Tickets are on sale through the theater; it's on our Events page.

buzz.headline: EsterEv adds an everyday, drop-in menu
buzz.body: EsterEv says it now has a regular menu built for walk-ins: the kind of night where you grab a few plates and a drink on a random Friday without making it a whole event. One of the new plates pairs rye toast with apple and shaved radish.

image.alt: A round toast topped with shaved radish, diced apple and herbs on a white plate

buzz.headline: Lefse before Thanksgiving: where does Bay View buy it?
buzz.body: With the holiday coming, a neighbor asked the group where to find lefse, the soft Norwegian potato flatbread that shows up on a lot of Midwest holiday tables. Commenters pointed toward a big-box grocer outside the neighborhood, so if a Bay View shop carries it, now's the time to speak up.

image.alt: A round of lefse spread with butter and sugar, rolled up on a flowered plate (stock photo)

history.title: The Hoan Bridge: Bay View's 'Bridge to Nowhere'
history.text: Built in the early 1970s, the Hoan Bridge sat finished but unconnected for years, mocked as the 'Bridge to Nowhere,' before it finally opened to traffic in 1977.
history.body:
The big steel arch that carries I-794 over the harbor mouth between downtown and Bay View grew out of 1960s freeway plans. City leaders had long wanted a high bridge along the lakefront, and the federal highway act of 1956 promised to pay most of the bill if it became part of the interstate system. First called the Harbor Bridge, it was soon named for Daniel Hoan, Milwaukee's longtime Socialist mayor.

Construction began in 1970, and accounts agree the main span was essentially done by about 1973 or 1974. But the freeways meant to feed it were in trouble. Opposition to a "ring of concrete" around downtown, and the fight against the Lake Freeway that would have carried traffic south along the lakefront, halted the connecting roads. With little to connect to, the finished bridge picked up a nickname that stuck for years: the "Bridge to Nowhere."

About $22 million in federal money finally completed the ramps, and the Hoan opened to traffic in 1977, according to Milwaukee Magazine. Its south end touched down at the edge of Bay View, and the Lake Parkway later extended the route farther south toward the suburbs.

The bridge has had a dramatic life since. In December 2000, two of the three main girders on one lakefront approach span cracked and the northbound deck sagged, closing those lanes for months; no one was hurt. A rehabilitation finished around 2016 was meant to add decades to its life, and since 2020 the arch has glowed at night with privately funded LED lights. This week it's in the news again: the Rethink 794 group's new boulevard plan for downtown keeps the Hoan connection.
